ann_42.text: This part acts on 68 of 242 training patients (28%); 38 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 65-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, 1 vessel coloured, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a normal thallium scan), it slightly lowers the predicted risk, from about 98% to about 94% (on the training data only).
Through it, older age (42 to 66 years) lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 26% to about 8%, and only once age rises above about 60 years (on the training data only).

ann_43.text: Through this part, higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 54% to about 6% (on the training data only).
It does so only once resting blood pressure rises above about 131 mm Hg (for the typical patient with a fold, from about 54% to about 4%; on the training data only).
An ST segment that is not upsloping raises the predicted risk here from about 26% to about 54% (on the training data only).

In the model as a whole, higher resting blood pressure clearly raises the predicted risk, and even more so if the ST segment is not upsloping (from about 37% to about 75%, against about 22% to about 29% with an upsloping one).

ann_44.text: This part acts on the 42 of 242 training patients (17%) with atypical angina; 8 of them had heart disease.
For the typical patient it acts on (a 52-year-old man with atypical angina and a normal thallium scan), it lowers the predicted risk from about 15% to about 7% (on the training data only).
Through it, atypical angina lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 26% to about 12% (on the training data only).

ann_45.text: This part acts on 59 of 242 training patients (24%); 19 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 55-year-old woman with atypical angina, an upsloping ST segment and a normal thallium scan), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from below 1% to about 2% (on the training data only).
Through it, atypical angina raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 26% to about 37% (on the training data only).

A downsloping ST segment and more vessels coloured raise it more with atypical angina (from about 7% to about 57%, and from about 7% to about 75%) than with other chest pain types (about 26% to about 54%, and about 26% to about 84%). The model has little data on this: only 17 training patients (a downsloping ST segment).
Being a woman clearly lowers it, and even more so without atypical angina (from about 26% to about 3%, against about 7% to about 1%).
For the typical patient it acts on, a downsloping ST segment raises it from about 2% to about 9% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this, 17 patients).

ann_46.text: This part acts on 142 of 242 training patients (59%); 82 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, 1.4 mm of ST depression, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a reversible defect on the thallium scan), it raises the predicted risk from about 89% to about 95% (on the training data only).
Through it, more ST depression on exercise (0 to 2.8 mm) raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 20% to about 70%, and only once it rises above about 0.4 mm (on the training data only).

ann_47.text: This part acts on 199 of 242 training patients (82%); 75 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 57-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, 0.3 mm of ST depression, an upsloping ST segment and a normal thallium scan), it raises the predicted risk from about 4% to about 32% (on the training data only).

Through it, more ST depression on exercise (0 to 2.8 mm) lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 46% to about 5%, and a flat ST segment lowers it from about 26% to about 5% (on the training data only).

Older age (42 to 66 years) raises it here from about 12% to about 41%, typical angina to about 39%, and a maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute from about 21% to about 30% (on the training data only).

Older age clearly raises it more if the ST segment is not flat (from about 7% to about 21%, against about 57% to about 60% with a flat one) and if ST depression is 0.8 mm or less (from about 12% to about 31%, against about 8% to about 18%).
In the model as a whole, more ST depression clearly raises the predicted risk, and even more so with a flat ST segment (from about 75% to about 94%, against about 38% to about 27% otherwise).

ann_48.text: Through this part, going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 26% to about 84%, a reversible thallium defect to about 51%, and higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) from about 17% to about 44% (on the training data only).
Being a woman lowers it to about 3%, and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 12% (on the training data only).
For two rare thallium results the model has little data on this: a result coded 4 (2 patients; about 79%) and a fixed defect (15 patients; about 15%), both on the training data only.
An abnormal resting ECG raises it only slightly here, from about 26% to about 30% (on the training data only).

ann_49.text: Through it, older age (42 to 66 years) slightly lowers a typical patient's predicted risk, from about 17% to about 12% (on the training data only).

ann_50.text: Through this part, an ST segment that is not upsloping raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 26% to about 54% (on the training data only).
Higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) raises it from about 22% to about 29% (on the training data only).

ann_51.text: Through this part, typical angina (about 4%) and non-anginal chest pain (about 7%) clearly lower a typical patient's predicted risk compared with no chest pain symptoms (about 26%).
Being a woman clearly lowers it, and even more so without chest pain symptoms (from about 26% to about 3%, against about 7% to about 1% with atypical angina).
More vessels coloured clearly raise it, and even more so with atypical angina (from 0 to 2 vessels, about 7% to about 75%, against about 26% to about 84% without chest pain symptoms).

A downsloping ST segment raises it, and even more so with atypical angina (from about 7% to about 57%, against about 26% to about 54%). The model has little data on this: only 17 training patients (a downsloping ST segment).

A thallium result coded 4 raises it, and even more so without chest pain symptoms (from about 26% to about 79%, against about 7% to about 31% with atypical angina). The model has little data on this: only 2 training patients (thallium stress test result coded 4 (meaning not recorded)).
Only 2 training patients have a thallium result coded 4.

ann_52.text: Through this part, older age (42 to 66 years) raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 12% to about 41%, a flat ST segment to about 42%, typical angina to about 39%, and chest pain brought on by exercise to about 38% (on the training data only).
A maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute lowers it here from about 31% to about 23% (on the training data only).

Age adds to the predicted risk through this part only once it rises above about 58 years, and only slightly (for the typical patient with a fold, from about 95% to about 97%; on the training data only).

ann_53.text: For a typical patient, the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina or non-anginal chest pain (about 7% each) than with no chest pain symptoms (about 26%).

Going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured raises a typical patient's predicted risk to about 84%, a flat ST segment to about 71%, a reversible thallium defect to about 51%, and higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) from about 17% to about 44% (on the training data only).

Being a woman lowers it to about 3%, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 12%, and a maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute gives about 23% rather than about 31% (on the training data only).

Older age (42 to 66 years) raises it from about 7% to about 21%, chest pain brought on by exercise to about 38%, and higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) from about 22% to about 29% (on the training data only).

summary.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms and median test results, predicted risk of heart disease about 26%), the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk with typical angina or non-anginal chest pain (about 7% each).

Going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured by fluoroscopy raises a typical patient's predicted risk to about 84%, a flat rather than upsloping ST segment to about 71%, a reversible defect on the thallium scan to about 51%, and higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) from about 17% to about 44% (on the training data only).
Being a woman lowers it to about 3%, and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 12% (on the training data only).

More ST depression on exercise clearly raises the predicted risk, and even more so if the ST segment is flat: going from 0 to 2.8 mm moves it from about 75% to about 94% with a flat ST segment, against about 38% to about 27% otherwise.
Older age (42 to 66 years) raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 7% to about 21%, and chest pain brought on by exercise raises it to about 38% (on the training data only).
For two rare thallium results the model has little data on this: a result coded 4 (2 patients; about 79%) and a fixed defect (15 patients; about 15%), both on the training data only.
